newsitem.title: UK: Russian Eurobonds held up by tax uncertainties.
newsitem.headline: Russian Eurobonds held up by tax uncertainties.

text.p: Confusion about the Russian tax system, which could mean bond investors paying an extra 35 percent in tax, is holding up the issue of new Russian eurobonds.
But bankers said on Wednesday that obstacles to issuance were easier to overcome for banks than companies or municipalities.
"Tax uncertainties are a factor in delaying Russian Eurobond issues," Stewart Naunton, tax partner at Coopers & Lybrand in Moscow said. "(But) it is easier to launch bonds for banks."
Eurobond investors buy withholding tax-exempt bonds so they are only liable for taxes in their country of residence.
This convention has allowed the international Eurobond market to flourish. But Russia charges a 15 percent withholding tax on all interest and dividend income.
This problem can be overcome by issuing bonds via a subsidiary in a country without withholding tax, such as the Netherlands, bankers said.
United Export Import Bank (Uneximbank) issued a $50 million private placement on Monday via its Dutch subsidiary Unexim International Finance BV.
"Issuing bonds through a Dutch subsidiary is a good way for Russian banks to access the international capital markets," said Heidi Credo at Merrill Lynch, lead of the Uneximbank deal.
"(But) there are different tax considerations for banks than corporates, particularly regarding securities issued."

Companies may not find it easy to obtain approval for a foreign subsidiary. They also have to go via the central bank, ministry of finance and the Federal Securities Commission, whereas banks need only get a green light from the central bank.
An added complication for corporates is a risk that interest paid on their bonds might be subject to 20 percent VAT.

"On balance, it is likely VAT does not apply to bonds," said Naunton at Coopers & Lybrand. "But under existing legislation it could apply, and that is a risk. Therefore transactions need to be structured accordingly."
Government borrowers cannot issue bonds via foreign subsidiaries, and it remains unclear how their paper will be exempt from withholding tax.
Russia's debut $1.0 billion Eurobond, launched last November, had a letter from the tax service and the ministry of finance clarifying the basis of taxation, and was exempt.

"For municipalities, there may have to be some form of repackaging (where the bonds are issued via a special purpose offshore company and the proceeds passed on) or Russia will have to legislate especially for them," a banker involved in the transactions said.
The recent introduction of a further 15 percent tax on earnings on government securities has put a spanner in the works for planned deals from municipalities Moscow and St Petersburg.
Questions about whether the tax applies to international as well as domestic bond issues, and rumours it might be repealed, need to be cleared up, bankers said.

Earlier this month, the chairman of St Petersburg's finance committee said it had been due to launch its debut bond by early February. The bond was delayed because investors would not buy the paper until they knew whether or not the new tax applied.
Russia itself is expected to issue a jumbo mark bond during the first quarter, and said it will raise a total of $1.5 billion internationally in 1997.
Bankers said the tax situation on its deals was also unclear, but "the dollar Eurobond indicates the government's line of thinking", they said.
But despite the likely delays and complications of issuing Eurobonds, the number of Russian borrowers planning deals continues to grow.
Uneximbank said on Tuesday it planned a public bond issue for up to $200 million by mid-year.

Gazprom GAZP.RUO, LUKoil LKOH.RTS, telephone company MGTS, power utility Mosenergo, Rostelekom, the Russian railways ministry as well as regions within Russia have all said they would like to tap the international debt markets.
